summary: Today’s pulse tracks Kraków shooting latest updates: six killed and more than a dozen injured, police say, Six dead after gunman opens fire ‘at random’ in Kraków market square, and Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors. Across Guardian, NPR, and BBC, the strongest repeated signals are injured, poland, and birth. In the background, Rise in NHS birth centre closures ‘shocking’ denial of women’s rights, experts say and Italian foreign minister says hackers leaked his personal data keep the wider picture in motion.

headlines.title: Kraków shooting latest updates: six killed and more than a dozen injured, police say
headlines.description: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk heads to the city after four women and two men are killed and more than a dozen people injured Tom Rose, the US ambassador to Poland, wrote on X: We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Kraków, a savage and murderous attack that’s shattered the peace of Poland. America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Kraków. A terrible tragedy in Kraków’s Main Market Square. I share the grief of the families and loved ones of the victims of this unimaginable tragedy. The perpetrator was injured and detained.

headlines.title: Six dead after gunman opens fire ‘at random’ in Kraków market square
headlines.description: Reports say man fired shots from from his car in Poland’s second city before being wounded by police while trying to flee Kraków shooting – latest updates Six people have been killed and 15 injured after a shooting in a market square in Kraków, Poland. A man who had driven into the square at about 3pm began “firing at random people from his car”, according to a statement by local police on X.

headlines.title: Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors
headlines.description: Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was removed from office and placed under house arrest Friday. The Senate voted on his impeachment after the collapse of a state-affiliated bank.

headlines.title: Rise in NHS birth centre closures ‘shocking’ denial of women’s rights, experts say
headlines.description: Twelve midwife-led maternity units have closed in England since 2019 with six closing since Labour came to power in 2024 NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a “shocking” denial of a woman’s right to have a midwife rather than a doctor oversee their baby’s birth, say campaigners. Twelve birth centres – midwife-led maternity units – have closed in England since 2019. Birth centres play a key role in ensuring that women can choose whether to have their baby at a unit in a hospital run by doctors, at one where midwives are in charge, or at home.

headlines.title: Italian foreign minister says hackers leaked his personal data
headlines.description: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has blamed pro-Russian hackers for publishing the details online.

headlines.title: Three teenagers arrested after 17-year-old injured in Gloucester sword attack
headlines.description: Armed police attended the scene, which led to two nearby schools going into lockdown Three teenagers have been arrested after a 17-year-old was injured in a suspected sword attack near a school in Gloucester. Officers were called to Chalford Road, near St Peter’s high school, in Tuffley, shortly after 8.50am on Friday. It was reported that two people, one in possession of a sword, had been seen chasing two 17-year-olds. The suspects then fled the scene on foot.

headlinePool.title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
headlinePool.description: Weeks of coalition talks could follow after preliminary results pointed to a highly divided national parliament.

headlinePool.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC
headlinePool.description: The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte".

headlinePool.title: Stephen Miller, Trump’s incoming chief of staff, pledges ‘total devotion’ to the president
headlinePool.description: Hardline aide offers ‘unwavering commitment’ to president amid fears White House will double down on far-right immigration agenda Stephen Miller, Donald Trump ’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, has lavished praise on the president after his appointment as White House chief of staff. In his first public remarks since the move was announced, Miller – who begins the role on Monday – pledged “total devotion” to Trump amid concern the administration is now poised to double down on its far-right, nativist immigration agenda.

headlinePool.title: National Trust votes to seek banking partner more in tune with its environmental policies
headlinePool.description: Charity’s AGM decides overwhelmingly to begin tendering process amid criticism of Barclays’ fossil fuel investments The National Trust has voted overwhelmingly to seek a new banking partner in a significant victory for members who have long argued that its relationship with Barclays was at odds with its commitment to protecting the natural world. The resolution, passed at the charity’s annual general meeting on Saturday with the backing of its board of trustees, instructs the organisation to begin a competitive tendering process for its banking arrangements.

headlinePool.title: Vetting candidates is a tricky process but Reform can’t seem to get it right
headlinePool.description: Charges against party members and off-piste remarks highlight problems brought about by rapid expansion Speaking to reporters after unveiling his new defence spokesperson this week, Nigel Farage’s jovial and upbeat mood suddenly switched. Why, he was asked, was a Reform UK councillor who was arrested in January over multiple alleged sexual offences still in his role nearly 10 months later? “I have no idea,” Farage replied icily. “I was told yesterday, and I wasn’t very happy.”

headlinePool.title: LA’s newer, bluer wave: Nithya Raman leads way as city’s progressives make their mark
headlinePool.description: Democratic socialists won the mayorship, a US House seat and powerful positions in Los Angeles – and a large network of volunteers helped them do it As a blue tsunami overtook US politics this week, Los Angeles saw a major shake-up of its own with a wave of democratic socialists elected to key offices. Most notably, Nithya Raman, the first democratic socialist to serve on the Los Angeles city council, prevailed over incumbent Karen Bass to become the next mayor. Even in the deep blue city, Raman’s victory was hardly a given, and marked a stunning win for the progressive wing of the party. With her election, America’s two largest cities will now be run by democratic socialist mayors.

headlinePool.title: ‘Life-changing’: parents welcome £10m UK play centre for disabled children
headlinePool.description: Gympanzees near Bristol will be the first UK site of its type, catering for children unable to use regular playgrounds It has been over a decade since Stephanie Wheen set out to create the UK’s first play and leisure centre specifically designed for disabled children. Over the past 10 years, she and her team have raised millions of pounds, meticulously researched how to make the centre as inclusive as possible and spent years trialling sessions with disabled children. And soon, the doors to Gympanzees will open for the first time.

headlinePool.title: A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
headlinePool.description: Doctors expected an experimental drug that lowers a common risk factor for heart attacks would save patients' lives. The medicine made no difference.

headlinePool.title: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’
headlinePool.description: National party will be largest in parliament but ultimate shape of next government won’t be settled for some time New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc. On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.
